messages.subject: increased computation time
parts:
Hello all! 

I use GGIR for an ongoing research project. I analyze raw data from axivity accelerometers. Usually we record about 3 weeks of 24h data recorded @ 50 Hz. So far I analyzed about 140 patients and it worked pretty well (about 45min for the whole analysis). Recently I received a new laptop with better computational power (Intel EVO i7, 16 gb RAM, before I only had 8gb) than my previous one, but the analysis of my data takes ages now (up to 2 hours)!.

I use the following setup: 
R Studio 2024.04.0
R 4.3.3 [64-bit]
GGIR version: 3.0.9

I remember that on my old laptop the CPU was usually pretty much "maxed out" during the analysis. Now it remains at ~ 40% capacity. RAM is around 80%. CPU does still max out if i do any other analysis (unrelated to GGIR) in R Studio that require intensive computation.

Any help or ideas highly appreciated! 

Best, 
Thomas

Here thedefinition of my g.shell.GGIR function: 

g.shell.GGIR(
  mode=c(1:5),
  datadir="C:/AXIVITY/raw",
  outputdir="C:/AXIVITY/analyzed",
  do.report=c(2,4,5),
  overwrite = TRUE,
  do.parallel=FALSE,
  ## call external function
  myfun = myfun,
  desiredtz = "Europe/Zurich",
  dynrange = 4,
  do.cal = FALSE,
 
  #=====================
  # Part 2
  #=====================
  strategy = 1,
  hrs.del.start = 0,          
  hrs.del.end = 0,
  maxdur = 40,                  
  includedaycrit = 12,

  # MX Metrics
  qwindow=c(0,24),
  qlevels=c(960/1440, 1320/1440, 1380/1440, 1410/1440, 1425/1440, 1435/1440, 1438/1440),
  mvpathreshold =c(100),
  bout.metric = 4,
  excludefirstlast = FALSE,
  includenightcrit = 12,
  minimum_MM_length = 23,
  MX.ig.min.dur = 10,
  #intensity gradient
  iglevels=TRUE,
 
 
  #=====================
  # Part 3 + 4
  #=====================
  def.noc.sleep = c(1),
  anglethreshold = 5,timethreshold = 5,
  outliers.only = FALSE,
  do.visual = FALSE,
  relyonsleeplog = FALSE,
  #=====================
  # Part 5
  #=====================
  threshold.lig = c(25), threshold.mod = c(100),  threshold.vig = c(425),
  boutcriter = 0.8,      boutcriter.in = 0.9,     boutcriter.lig = 0.8,
  boutcriter.mvpa = 0.8, boutdur.in = c(1,10,30), boutdur.lig = c(1,10),
  boutdur.mvpa = c(1,10),
 
  includedaycrit.part5 = 2/3,
  #=====================
  # Visual report
  #=====================
  timewindow = c("MM","WW"),
  visualreport=c(TRUE))

messages.author: 5270e62a7d3ec577
messages.subject: Re: increased computation time
parts:
Hi Thomas,

Although you have more RAM, you are likely splitting it over more CPU cores than you were before, which can result in slower processing speeds. For example my work laptop has 12 virtual cores and 16Gb ram. If you let GGIR run by default it will use the max N CPU cores - 1 (so 11 for me) and split the RAM between that. Compared with an older model CPU which may have had 4 cores, 8gb RAM and therefore 8/3 is higher than 16/11....so the older PC may well run faster in this scenario as you experienced.

There is a way to tweak this though - you can use maxNcores = x within the GGIR function to tune this. I allow for 2gb per core typically, and often just set the cores to 6 so that I can still use the PC for other work. Depending on your CPU physical and virtual cores (if you have hyperthreading on your CPU for example), you will need to adjust to get the best balance for performance and ability to use the PC if it's your only one. To throw another curve ball into the mix, some of the newer CPU's also are having a mix of threads which are Performance-cores (P-cores) or flexible Efficient-cores (E-cores) which may further cause tweaking to your setup. 

My apologies if any of this comes across as patronizing, I'm being thorough to benefit others in the community that may have this issue in the future.  

Hope that helps!

Thanks,
Ben

messages.author: 017566be30afa7f3
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Re: increased computation time
parts:
Hi Ben and Thomas,

I am not sure I understand why this solved the issue. My understanding is that if we allocate less cores the actual amount of memory per core will stay the same, we are just able to process less files in parallel. For example, you now have 16/12 gb per core both with maxNcores = 11 and with maxNcores = 6. So, speed should not change. Maybe it worked for you because your operating system struggled to do other work next to GGIR and that slows everything down? (I am not an expert in this, so just guessing).

Ben, what do you mean by "I allow for 2gb per core typically"? Do you mean you plugged in an extra memory card or are you referring to job parameters in a cluster where you can indeed set memory requirements which is harder on a desktop computer?

Either way, it would be good to make sure GGIR users in general can find helpful directions on how to maximise the processing speed. Currently we have as guidance: https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/chapter2_Pipeline.html#processing-time

In the 4th bullet point I highlight changing parameter chunksize, which I think would be a good additional one to consider. By the way I now see the typo there in do.paralllel = FALSE and will fix that soon.

Thanks,

Vincent

parts:
Hi Vincent,

Some of my description may be slightly off, I'm going off my experience building my own desktop computers and having to consider the optimum hardware mix for performance. I think there is something to be said for reducing the number of cores if doing anything, particularly on laptops which tend to have much lower clock speeds on the CPU's at ~1.8GHz and hyperthreading becoming the norm. There are also the demands of just running the OS in the background to consider even if you aren't doing anything tangible on it.

Changing the chunk size is a suitable alternative as you suggest, though I've not tested it myself in this scenario. Thanks for linking the processing time info, I don't think it was as thorough last time I saw otherwise I would have directed Thomas there directly!

Thanks,
Ben
